editor_spans.body: Fares frozen 'for the first time in 30 years' is a quiet admission of what is being undone. Thirty years ago was the privatisation of British Rail. Great British Railways is less a new idea than a reassembly of the integrated railway that the 1990s broke into franchises and infrastructure.

The Derby headquarters will not be finished until spring 2029 and will house up to 450 staff. That makes 'hundreds of rail jobs' accurate but modest. The building is a symbol of where the railway is run from; whether passengers see better service depends on decisions that the HQ itself will not make.

The more revealing figure sits further down: less than 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. That is the long shadow of decades with little coordinated training across a fragmented industry. Up to 600 apprentices over four years is a start against an ageing workforce, not a solution to it.

Read together, the week's Ukraine statements show Britain running two messages at once. It 'fully supports' the US-led track and Trump's energy ceasefire. It also insists Russia has repeatedly rejected ceasefires and 'has no interest in peace'. London is hedging against a Washington-brokered deal it cannot shape.

There is a domestic motive too. The Prime Minister framed the energy ceasefire as the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets. The government's own response pairs Ukraine with energy prices and the cost of living. Support for Kyiv is being argued partly through household bills.

The scale deserves perspective. £1.6 billion for more than 5,000 missiles over four years is the real commitment. The 'acceleration' for this winter is £10 million of it. Ukraine is entering its fifth winter under bombardment, and the gap between rhetoric of 'further and faster' and the sums actually moved is worth watching.
A Prime Minister who built his reputation as a metro mayor is now exporting that model. 'No10 North' and the push for regional power in Scotland follow the logic of English combined authorities.

Aiming the push at Holyrood rather than Westminster is politically pointed. Twenty-seven years after devolution, Burnham casts the Scottish Government as one of Europe's most centralised administrations. That turns devolution's own argument against its first beneficiary.
Whether the 'offer' is genuine will be tested by what Westminster is prepared to fund and cede directly, not by what it asks Edinburgh to give up.

The EU summit list is essentially an inventory of the frictions created in 2016–2020. It includes salmon checks, banned seed potatoes and burgers, export certificates, and lost criminal-record sharing.

The bigger signal is the call for a 'serious dialogue' on the long-term relationship, paired with the assurance that the public will be 'the boss'. After 'a decade of drift and division', the government is testing whether opinion has moved far enough to reopen the question without reopening the wound.
